diagnosis: Ossifying fibroma arising in hyperparathyroidism–jaw tumour syndrome
legend: There is a relatively avascular hypercellular stroma composed of bland spindled cells associated with bony trabeculae.

The morphological features of parafibromin-deficient parathyroid tumours are inconsistent but include a thickened and somewhat hyalinized fibrous capsule, a sheet-like growth pattern, eosinophilic cells, and prominent vasculature. A little microcystic change is noted.

In contrast to most usual parathyroid adenomas, which demonstrate a somewhat nested architecture, parafibromin-deficient parathyroid tumours commonly show a sheet-like architecture with prominent vasculature.
Cytological features include nuclear enlargement, perinuclear cytoplasmic clearing, and eosinophilic cells.
Cytological features include nuclear enlargement often with preserved N:C ratios, multinucleation, perinuclear cytoplasmic clearing, and eosinophilic cells, sometimes with a glassy quality.

diagnosis: Adenosarcoma of the uterus arising in hyperparathyroidism–jaw tumour syndrome
legend: There is a densely hypercellular stroma surrounding entrapped glands.

diagnosis: Adenosarcoma of the uterus arising in hyperparathyroidism–jaw tumour syndrome
legend: Parafibromin immunohistochemistry has not been well validated as a diagnostic marker of adenosarcoma in the setting of hyperparathyroidism–jaw tumour syndrome. However, in this case, the stromal component of the adenosarcoma demonstrates loss of nuclear expression that contrasts with the preserved expression in the glandular component and the adjacent non-neoplastic stroma.

Immunohistochemistry for parafibromin can be difficult to interpret. It is emphasized that significance is placed on nuclear expression only, and nonspecific cytoplasmic expression should be disregarded. In this case, all the neoplastic cells show loss of expression of parafibromin and there is preserved expression in non-neoplastic cells. Therefore, the tumour is considered parafibromin-deficient.

diagnosis: Parathyroid carcinoma associated with hyperparathyroidism–jaw tumour syndrome
legend: The diagnosis of carcinoma arising in the setting of hyperparathyroidism–jaw tumour syndrome relies on the same histological criteria as sporadic carcinomas: the demonstration of unequivocally invasive growth or vascular space invasion. In this instance, in addition to invasive growth, the neoplastic cells show typical cytological features of a parafibromin-deficient tumour.
It is emphasized that for parafibromin immunohistochemistry to be considered negative there should be an internal positive control in non-neoplastic cells including non-neoplastic parathyroid tissue.
This non-invasive parafibromin-deficient parathyroid tumour shows typical features including a sheet-like growth of cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm and microcystic change.
